prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which established the incretin principle and enabled GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B028 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case rests on the discovery chain and not on the unanimous opening ranking. Proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action and its extrapancreatic effects defined what any therapy would have to mimic. The resulting drug class has confirmed benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal outcomes in large independent trials. No member found a maturity or timing problem, and I agree. The chair asks whether the citation should reward physiology and peptide identification or also drug development. I hold that the prize honours a discovery that changed a field, and the discovery is the hormone biology. The therapeutic consequence belongs in the citation as the reason the discovery matters, not as a separate laureate seat. The trio Drucker, Holst and Mojsov covers human incretin physiology, GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and the active peptide form, which fits that reading within three names.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and the round-1 exchange has not resolved it. Habener is not among the credited names and every member flagged this, so each trio can be challenged. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested, and nothing in the supplied text lets me settle it. A discovery-only trio leaves out Knudsen, whose work produced liraglutide and semaglutide, and a committee that gives weight to development could fairly reject my choice. I also accept El Manira's and Linnarsson's concern that a prize for a drug class with a large commercial footprint may be read as rewarding commercial success, and that safety and durability after discontinuation are not fully settled. If the committee cannot defend Mojsov's seat from the record, my configuration loses its main justification.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Knudsen as the third name, argues that converting native GLP-1 into a once-weekly drug needed new insight on albumin binding and DPP-4 resistance, and says he would not treat the choice as a point of principle.
responses.response: His argument moves me part of the way, because it shows that the long-acting analogue was not routine engineering. I still read the prize as honouring a discovery that changed the field, and the discovery that made the drug possible is the physiology and the active peptide. The albumin-binding step is a major contribution but it builds on a known mechanism. If four or more members side with Knudsen in the third seat, I would accept Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as a defensible outcome. My own preference is that Mojsov's identification of the peptide is the scientific discovery on which the therapies rest, so I do not change my configuration, and I would ask that the citation then name the therapeutic consequence so that the development step is acknowledged.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, reasoning that the citation should reward discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form and not a company's drug design.
responses.response: I agree with his movement, and with the reason he gives. I would add one caution. Moving because five colleagues proposed the trio is not itself a scientific argument, and I would not want the committee to treat the count that way. The argument for Mojsov is that identification and synthesis of the active peptide is a documented step on which the physiology and the drugs depend. On his round-2 question about a second part, I do not support adding one. The three-name limit is already used, and any second part would force a smaller GLP-1 set that none of us has defended.

responses.point: Sandberg says neither the rules nor precedent excludes an industry scientist and that the issue is the nature of the contribution, and he would reconsider Knudsen first among the alternatives for the third seat.
responses.response: I agree that employment in industry is not an exclusion, and I do not rest my case on it. What I weigh is the type of contribution. Knudsen's work is design and optimisation of a known peptide, and by that standard it is a different kind of step from identification of the active form. That said, I accept his point that omitting her could be read as honouring physiology and ignoring the step that reached patients. This is the strongest argument against my trio, and it is a reason to word the citation carefully, not a reason to change the names. I also share his unverified recollection of the priority history, and I would not want the committee to treat either of us as authority on it.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the peptide is documented well enough to justify credit and that excluding her risks a mistake the field would remember, while also noting that B045 has a cleaner June and Sadelain pairing with fewer credit problems.
responses.response: I agree on Mojsov, and her point about the cost of excluding her is what I weigh most heavily. On B045 I accept that June and Sadelain is a cleaner pairing than B028 in credit terms, with durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancy. I keep CAR-T as my first alternative for that reason. It does not change my choice for this year, because the B028 case is stronger on completeness and confirmation, and cleaner attribution does not make a weaker case stronger. Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and TIL work is a separate lineage, and Eshhar's omission is unresolved, so I would not support the full credited trio for B045.

responses.point: El Manira ranks B020 (Walter and Mori) as his second choice for its clean attribution and decades of confirmation, and would hold CAR-T for a year until the committee agrees on what the achievement is.
responses.response: I agree that B020 has the cleanest attribution on the list and the strongest basic-science case. Svenningsson's point that the citation would have to concentrate on the IRE1, HAC1 and XBP1 mechanism, and that therapeutic translation is thin, is fair, and I take it into account. Because of it I now list B020 as my second alternative alongside B045, replacing B014. My concern about B014 is unchanged: six names for three seats, with priority split between channel discovery and neuronal application. I do not think that can be solved by any selection of three names. B020 and B014 are different kinds of claim, and I would prefer B020 for a later year over a forced three-name optogenetics prize.

uncertainties: Fair allocation among Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen and the uncredited Habener cannot be resolved from the supplied text, and my recollection of the priority history is unverified.
Whether the committee prefers to honour discovery only or to include development. This decides the third name and the citation wording.
Whether the record supports Mojsov's priority for the active peptide well enough to hold the third seat. If it does not, Knudsen is the next most defensible name.
Whether the commercial footprint of the drug class affects how a GLP-1 prize is read, and whether long-term safety and durability after discontinuation are settled enough.
Whether a later second part for B020 or B045 would be better than one now. The three-name limit makes a two-part prize this year hard to defend.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist is apparent. My nuclear receptor work with Ronald Evans and my dopamine neuron research do not overlap with the shortlisted achievements. I have co-authored with colleagues Svenningsson and El Manira (and a shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation with other members). These are collegial ties that do not involve any shortlisted candidate, so I report no recusal issue.
